title: The rise and fall of Napoleon
blurb: From a Corsican boyhood and the Revolution to the coup of 1799, Waterloo and St Helena: the battles, the reforms that outlived him, and the cost in lives across Europe and beyond.

steps.c: Napoleone di Buonaparte was born in the family house in Ajaccio on 15 August 1769, a year after Genoa ceded Corsica to France. His parents, Carlo and Letizia, were minor nobles of Tuscan origin; Carlo had backed Pasquale Paoli's independent Corsica, then made his peace with the French, whose governor Marbeuf became his patron and the boy's godfather. At home the children spoke Corsican and Italian; French came later, at school.

tips.t: On 8 May 1769 French troops crushed Paoli's Corsicans at Ponte Novu, and Paoli went into exile in Britain. The Bonapartes, who had helped him, stayed and swore loyalty to Louis XV.
By the Treaty of Versailles of 1768 the Republic of Genoa, unable to put down the Corsican rebellion, ceded the island to France.

img_alt.file: File:Carlo Buonaparte.jpg
img_alt.by: Attributed to Anton Raphael Mengs, c. 1766–1779 (presumed portrait of Carlo Buonaparte)

steps.c: In 1779, aged nine, he was sent to France: first to a school at Autun to learn French, then to the military academy at Brienne-le-Château, where boys mocked his accent, his birthplace and his size. He withdrew into books, excelled at mathematics and became a fervent Corsican nationalist. A famous story has him leading the younger boys to victory in a snowball fight, but it may be legend. After a year at the École militaire in Paris he was commissioned in September 1785, aged 16, as a second lieutenant of artillery at Valence.

tips.t: His father died in February 1785, leaving the family short of money, so he finished the two-year course in one. Examined by the scientist Laplace, he was the first Corsican to graduate from the École militaire.
With his regiment at Auxonne he worked on a history of Corsica and sent it to his hero Paoli, who found it amateurish and too impassioned.

img_alt.file: File:The Young Napoleon at Military Academy in Brienne France 1779.jpg

steps.c: The Revolution thrilled him, and he spent more time on leave in Corsica than with his regiment: an active Jacobin, he became lieutenant colonel of a battalion of Corsican volunteers in 1792. In February 1793 he served in a failed French attack on La Maddalena off Sardinia. His family then fell out with Paoli, now ruling Corsica: Paolists detained him and sacked the family house, and in June 1793 the Buonapartes fled to Toulon as refugees. The Corsican patriot was becoming a Frenchman.

tips.t: At La Maddalena the young officer wanted a night attack but was overruled; when the attack was called off, too few boats came and his men had to spike and abandon their cannon.

In July 1793 he wrote 'Le souper de Beaucaire', a pamphlet in which a soldier argues merchants out of rebellion against the Republic. It had little effect, but it pleased the Jacobin deputies who could advance his career.

img_alt.file: File:Henri Félix Emmanuel Philippoteaux - Portrait of Napoleon Bonaparte.jpg
img_alt.by: Henri Félix Emmanuel Philippoteaux, 1835 (Bonaparte as lieutenant colonel of Corsican volunteers, 1792)

steps.c: In September 1793 his fellow Corsican Saliceti, a deputy of the Convention, had the 24-year-old captain made artillery commander at the siege of Toulon, which royalists had handed to the British. Bonaparte saw that guns on the heights by the forts of L'Éguillette and Balaguier could cut the harbour off from the allied fleet, and he trained infantrymen to serve his batteries. In the night assault of 16–17 December he was bayoneted in the thigh; the allies sailed away and Toulon fell on 19 December. He was promoted brigadier general at 24, while the victors shot up to 800 royalist prisoners in the town.

tips.t: Toulon brought him to the attention of Augustin Robespierre, younger brother of Maximilien. In February 1794 he became artillery commander of the Army of Italy, based at Nice.
As they left Toulon, British and Spanish forces burned or carried off several French warships, crippling much of the French navy for a time.

img_alt.file: File:Napoleon à Toulon par Edouard Detaille.jpg
img_alt.by: Édouard Detaille, Bonaparte at the siege of Toulon (Musée de l'Armée)

steps.t: Out of favour, then cannon in Paris
steps.c: The fall of Robespierre nearly ended his career: as Augustin Robespierre's protégé he was arrested on 9 August 1794 and held for two weeks. In 1795 he refused a posting against the royalist rebels of the Vendée and in September was struck off the list of serving generals. Three weeks later, on 13 Vendémiaire (5 October 1795), Barras made him his second in command against a royalist rising in Paris: Bonaparte had Murat fetch 40 cannon and fired canister into the crowds by the church of Saint-Roch. 'A whiff of grapeshot' is the historian Carlyle's later phrase; by the end of October Bonaparte commanded the Army of the Interior.

tips.t: In July 1794 Augustin Robespierre sent him to the Republic of Genoa to find out its intentions towards France; days after his return came Thermidor and his arrest.
In April 1795 he was posted to the Army of the West, fighting the royalist rising in the Vendée, as an infantry general. He would not go.

img_alt.file: File:Pierre Goetsbloets, vol. 3, Massacre à Paris le 13 vendemiaire l'an 4me de la republique - les troupes de lignes et gardes nationales se battent contre les sections de Paris le jour de dimanche 4 octobre 1795.jpg

steps.c: He fell for Joséphine de Beauharnais, a Caribbean-born widow of the Terror and former mistress of Barras; they married on 9 March 1796, and two days later he left to command the ragged Army of Italy, where whole battalions lacked shoes. Writing her a stream of passionate letters, he knocked Piedmont out of the war in two weeks and beat the Austrians at Lodi, Arcole and Rivoli. Over 110 works of art went to Paris in 1796 alone, and two army newspapers, one for his troops and one for France, built his legend. In October 1797 he signed the peace of Campo Formio himself, partitioning the Republic of Venice with Austria.

tips.t: On 10 May 1796 French columns stormed the bridge over the Adda; when the column faltered, Masséna, Berthier, Lannes and other officers rushed to its head. The fight became a core of the Napoleonic legend and convinced Bonaparte himself that he was destined for great things.

In November 1796 he seized a flag to lead an attack on the bridge at Arcole; his aide Muiron was killed beside him and he ended up in a muddy ditch. Gros's famous portrait shows only the heroic moment.

img_alt.file: File:Battle of Lodi, 10 May 1796 (by Louis-François Lejeune).jpg

steps.c: To strike at Britain's trade with India, he sailed from Toulon on 19 May 1798 with about 36,000 troops, seized Malta on the way and landed at Alexandria on 28 June. He beat the Mamluks near the pyramids on 21 July, but on 1 August Nelson destroyed his fleet in Aboukir Bay, cutting the army off from France. With him came 167 scholars of the Commission of Sciences and Arts, whose survey became the great Description de l'Égypte. He later boasted that in Egypt he had made himself 'a Moslem' to rule.
steps.w: French invasion of Egypt and Syria

tips.t: In the Battle of the Nile the French flagship L'Orient, which had carried Bonaparte from Toulon, caught fire and exploded at around 10 pm.
With scholars of the Commission, Bonaparte rode three days across the desert to Suez. One aim of the scholars was to open a canal to the Red Sea.

img_alt.file: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Bonaparte Before the Sphinx.jpg

steps.t: Jaffa, Acre and a quiet exit
steps.c: In February 1799 he marched into Ottoman Syria with about 14,000 men. At Jaffa in March his troops sacked the town and he had the surrendered prisoners shot or bayoneted on the beach: about 2,440 or 4,100, depending on the source. Plague spread in the army and the siege of Acre, defended by Jezzar Pasha with British help, failed after two months; whether he had some plague victims poisoned with opium on the retreat is still debated. On 24 August 1799 he slipped away from Egypt without orders, leaving Kléber in command, and landed at Fréjus on 9 October.

tips.t: The army learned from a proclamation on 23 August that he had handed command to Kléber. He sailed on the frigate Muiron, named after his aide killed at Arcole.
He landed at Fréjus on 9 October 1799, officially to defend the Directory. A month later he overthrew it.

img_alt.file: File:Antoine-Jean Gros - Bonaparte visitant les pestiférés de Jaffa.jpg
img_alt.by: Antoine-Jean Gros, 1804 (propaganda: Bonaparte touching a plague victim at Jaffa)

steps.c: Back from his Egyptian expedition, General Bonaparte overthrew the Directory on 9–10 November 1799 (18–19 Brumaire). When the Council of Five Hundred at Saint-Cloud shouted him down, his brother Lucien called in the grenadiers. A new constitution made him First Consul, and a plebiscite approved it. Ten years of revolution ended in the rule of one man.

tips.t: In July 1799 French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone near Rashid in Egypt. The British took it in 1801; it has been in the British Museum since 1802.
The Banque de France was founded in January 1800. With the franc germinal of 1803 it gave France a stable currency for over a century.

img_alt.file: File:Bouchot - Le general Bonaparte au Conseil des Cinq-Cents.jpg

steps.c: In May 1800 Bonaparte led an army over the Great St Bernard Pass into Austrian-held Italy. At Marengo on 14 June the battle was nearly lost by midday; Desaix's division arrived in the evening and turned it, though Desaix was killed. Moreau's victory at Hohenlinden in December forced Austria to make peace at Lunéville in 1801.

tips.t: On 3 December 1800 Moreau beat the Austrians in the snowy forests east of Munich; Austria lost 13,550–15,500 men, most of them captured.
David's 'Napoleon Crossing the Alps' shows him on a rearing horse in a storm; in reality the crossing was made in fine weather, led by a guide on a mule.

img_alt.file: File:Lejeune - Bataille de Marengo.jpg

steps.c: To restore French control of Saint-Domingue, Napoleon sent his brother-in-law Leclerc with about 30,000 men in 1801–02. Toussaint Louverture was tricked, deported and died in a Jura prison in April 1803, and a law of May 1802 kept slavery in other French colonies and was forced back on Guadeloupe. But yellow fever destroyed the army, including Leclerc. After Vertières (18 November 1803) Dessalines declared Haiti independent on 1 January 1804 - the first state born of a successful slave revolt.

tips.t: Rather than surrender to the troops restoring slavery, Louis Delgrès and his followers blew themselves up at Matouba on 28 May 1802.
With Saint-Domingue lost, Napoleon sold Louisiana to the United States for $15 million in 1803, doubling the size of the country.

img_alt.file: File:Battle for Palm Tree Hill.jpg

steps.t: Order at home: Concordat and Code civil
steps.c: The Consulate rebuilt the state. The Concordat of 1801 made peace with the Catholic Church: the state paid and appointed bishops, and church lands sold in the Revolution stayed sold. The Code civil of 21 March 1804 gave all men equality before the law, secure property and civil marriage - but made wives subordinate to their husbands. Prefects, lycées (1802) and the Légion d'honneur (1802) still shape France today.

tips.t: The Concordat was signed on 15 July 1801. It lasted until 1905 and is still in force in Alsace and Moselle, which were German in 1905.
Louisiana's civil law, unlike that of other US states, still follows the French civil-law tradition shaped by the Code.

img_alt.file: File:Napoleon mauzaisse-1833.jpg

steps.c: On 2 December 1804 Napoleon was crowned Emperor of the French in Notre-Dame. Pope Pius VII had come from Rome, but Napoleon placed the crown on his own head and then crowned Joséphine. A plebiscite had approved the empire by a huge majority. David's painting of the scene is almost 10 metres wide.

tips.t: Beethoven had meant his Third Symphony for Bonaparte; by his pupil Ries' account he withdrew the dedication when he heard of the empire. It premiered in Vienna as the 'Eroica' in 1805.
On 26 May 1805 Napoleon took the Iron Crown of Lombardy in Milan Cathedral and became King of Italy.

img_alt.file: File:Jacques-Louis David - The Coronation of Napoleon (1805-1807).jpg

steps.c: For two years an army of up to about 200,000 men waited at Boulogne to invade England. It never crossed. On 21 October 1805 Nelson's 27 ships of the line met 33 French and Spanish ships off Cape Trafalgar: 18 were taken or destroyed, about 4,400 Franco-Spanish sailors were killed, and Nelson died of a musket wound. Britain ruled the seas for the rest of the war.

tips.t: The first Légion d'honneur awards to soldiers were handed out at the Boulogne camp on 16 August 1804.
A gale after the battle wrecked or scattered most of the captured ships off Cádiz.

img_alt.file: File:Turner, The Battle of Trafalgar (1822).jpg

steps.c: The Grande Armée marched from the Channel to the Danube in about a month and trapped an Austrian army at Ulm, where about 27,000 men surrendered on 20 October. On 2 December, a year after the coronation, Napoleon beat the Russian and Austrian emperors at Austerlitz: about 9,000 French against 27,000–36,000 allied losses. In 1806 he organised the Confederation of the Rhine, and Francis II ended the thousand-year Holy Roman Empire.

tips.t: Francis II laid down the crown of the Holy Roman Empire on 6 August 1806; he remained Emperor of Austria.
The Arc de Triomphe was ordered in 1806 after Austerlitz; it was finished only in 1836.

img_alt.file: File:La bataille d'Austerlitz. 2 decembre 1805 (François Gérard).jpg

steps.c: Prussia went to war in 1806 and was crushed in a single day: on 14 October Napoleon won at Jena while Davout, outnumbered more than two to one, beat the main Prussian army at Auerstedt. Napoleon entered Berlin on 27 October. From there, on 21 November, he issued the Berlin Decree, closing the Continent to British trade.

tips.t: The philosopher Hegel, finishing his 'Phenomenology of Spirit' in Jena, wrote on 13 October 1806 that he had seen the emperor, 'this world-soul', ride through the town.
Napoleon had the Quadriga taken from the Brandenburg Gate to Paris; it came back to Berlin in 1814.

img_alt.file: File:Charles Meynier - Entrée de Napoléon à Berlin. 27 octobre 1806.jpg

steps.t: Tilsit, the blockade and sugar from beets
steps.c: After the bloody draw at Eylau and victory at Friedland, Napoleon and Tsar Alexander met on a raft on the Niemen. At Tilsit Prussia lost about half its land, new states appeared (the Duchy of Warsaw, Jérôme's Kingdom of Westphalia), and Russia joined the Continental System. Cut off from cane sugar, Europe turned to sugar beet: Achard's first beet-sugar factory had opened in Silesia in 1801, and France built up a beet-sugar industry that still exists. Smugglers ran British goods in through hubs like Heligoland.

tips.t: Britain took Heligoland from Denmark in 1807 and used it as a depot for goods smuggled into the Continent.
Napoleon visited Benjamin Delessert's refinery at Passy in 1812, where Quéruel had developed industrial beet-sugar making; Delessert was made a baron.

img_alt.file: File:Treaty of Tilsit.jpg

steps.c: In 1808 Napoleon forced the Spanish Bourbons to abdicate at Bayonne and made his brother Joseph king. Madrid rose on 2 May; the next day hundreds of people were shot. All Spain revolted: at Bailén in July about 17,000 French soldiers surrendered, and Zaragoza resisted two sieges street by street. Partisan bands fought a 'little war', a guerrilla, and the war cost Spain about 300,000 dead. Goya painted 'The Third of May 1808' in 1814.

tips.t: In the winter of 1808–09 a British army retreated over the Galician mountains to Corunna and was taken off by sea; its commander Sir John Moore was killed.
Goya also etched 'The Disasters of War', 82 prints of atrocities on both sides; they were published only in 1863, after his death.

img_alt.file: File:El Tres de Mayo, by Francisco de Goya, from Prado (cropped).jpg

steps.c: Austria tried again in 1809. Napoleon took Vienna but was thrown back across the Danube at Aspern-Essling in May, his first personal defeat in a decade. Six weeks later, at Wagram, about 300,000 men fought for two days and each side lost some 35,000-39,000. In 1810 he married the Austrian emperor's daughter Marie Louise; his empire reached its greatest extent in 1811-12.

tips.t: Tyrolean peasants under the innkeeper Andreas Hofer rose against Bavarian rule in 1809; he was shot in Mantua in February 1810.
After Wagram Austria's Adriatic lands became France's Illyrian Provinces, with their capital at Ljubljana.

img_alt.file: File:Napoléon à Wagram - Horace Vernet.jpg

steps.c: Napoleon's seizure of the Spanish crown in 1808 left Spain's American empire without a legitimate king. Towns set up their own juntas - Caracas on 19 April 1810, Buenos Aires on 25 May 1810 - and on 5 July 1811 Venezuela declared independence. The Spanish American wars of independence had begun; by 1826 almost all of mainland Spanish America was free.

tips.t: Fleeing Junot's army in 1807, the Portuguese royal family sailed to Brazil; Rio de Janeiro was the capital of the Portuguese empire until 1821.
On 16 September 1810 the priest Miguel Hidalgo called his parishioners to revolt, starting Mexico's war of independence.

img_alt.file: File:Firma del acta de independencia de Venezuela.jpg

steps.c: When Russia left the Continental System, Napoleon invaded. On 24 June 1812 his main army - 422,000 men by Minard's count, part of some 600,000 or more in all - crossed the Niemen. Heat, hunger, typhus and desertion shrank it to about 100,000 by Moscow. At Borodino on 7 September, the bloodiest day of the wars, the two armies lost roughly 70,000-95,000 men (debated). Napoleon entered Moscow on 14 September; fires destroyed much of the city.

tips.t: The French took Smolensk on 17-18 August after a bombardment that set the old city on fire.
Fires raged from 14 to 18 September 1812 in the mostly wooden city; the governor Rostopchin is often held responsible.

img_alt.file: File:Battle of Borodino.jpg

steps.t: The retreat, as Minard drew it
steps.c: Napoleon left Moscow on 19 October. Forced back on the stripped road he had come by, the army starved and froze; at the Berezina (26-29 November) pontonniers stood in icy water to build two bridges. In 1869 Charles Minard drew the campaign as a band whose width shows the men: 422,000 out, 100,000 at Moscow, 4,000 back at the Niemen (10,000 with a northern corps). His figures are debated - Riehn counts 685,000 men entering Russia and fewer than 70,000 known survivors - but the shape of the disaster is clear.

tips.t: A mass grave of Grande Armée soldiers found in Vilnius in 2001 held lice carrying the bacteria of trench fever and typhus.
Tolstoy's novel, published 1865-1869 and written at Yasnaya Polyana, follows Russian families through 1805-1812 and the burning of Moscow.

img_alt.file: File:Napoleons retreat from Moscow by Adolph Northen.jpg

steps.t: Leipzig and the fall of Paris
steps.c: Prussia rose in 1813, with volunteers and a new citizen army inspired by German nationalism; Austria and Sweden joined Russia and Britain. At Leipzig on 16-19 October more than half a million men fought the 'Battle of the Nations', the largest battle in Europe before 1914. The allies invaded France in 1814 and Paris capitulated on 31 March. Napoleon abdicated at Fontainebleau on 6 April and was sent to rule the island of Elba.

tips.t: On 20 April 1814 Napoleon said goodbye to the Old Guard in the courtyard of Fontainebleau, kissing the flag before leaving for Elba.
Wellington routed Joseph Bonaparte's army at Vitoria on 21 June 1813, capturing 151 guns and the king's baggage; the French were driven back over the Pyrenees.

img_alt.file: File:Declaration of victory after the Battle of Leipzig, 1813 (by Johann Peter Krafft).jpg

steps.c: From November 1814 the Congress of Vienna redrew the map: a German Confederation of 39 states, a united Netherlands, a Russian-ruled Kingdom of Poland, Austria back in northern Italy. On 26 February 1815 Napoleon slipped away from Elba with about 1,000 men and landed at Golfe-Juan. At Laffrey the troops sent to stop him went over to him; on 20 March he was back in the Tuileries. The Congress declared him an outlaw and the allies mobilised again.

tips.t: His road over the Alps via Digne, Sisteron and Gap to Grenoble is now the N85 'Route Napoléon'.
In February 1815 the Congress powers declared the Atlantic slave trade 'repugnant to the principles of humanity', though without a date for ending it.

img_alt.file: File:Retour de Napoleon d' Isle d'Elbe, by Charles de Steuben.jpg

steps.c: Napoleon struck into Belgium to beat his enemies one by one. He beat the Prussians at Ligny on 16 June, but they retreated towards Wavre, not home. On 18 June at Waterloo, Wellington's army held the ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean all afternoon until Blücher's Prussians arrived on the French flank; the Imperial Guard's last attack failed and the army broke. About 24,000 allied and 26,000 French soldiers were killed or wounded. Napoleon abdicated again on 22 June.

tips.t: At the walled farm of Hougoumont alone the French lost about 5,000 of 12,700 men engaged.
On 15 July 1815 Napoleon surrendered to Captain Maitland of HMS Bellerophon off Rochefort.

img_alt.file: File:Battle of Waterloo 1815.PNG

steps.c: Napoleon spent his last years at Longwood House on St Helena, in the South Atlantic, dictating the memoirs that built his legend; he died on 5 May 1821, aged 51. His Code shaped civil law across Europe, Latin America and the Middle East, and his wars stirred nationalism in Germany, Italy and Spain and set Latin America on the road to independence. They also killed an estimated 3.5 to 7 million soldiers and civilians (figures debated), and about 2.3 million Frenchmen were called up in 1800-1815.

tips.t: In December 1840 Napoleon's body was brought back from St Helena and buried under the dome of Les Invalides in Paris.
In 1822 Champollion, working from the Rosetta Stone found during Bonaparte's Egyptian campaign, announced how hieroglyphs work.

img_alt.file: File:Carl von Steuben - Mort de Napoléon - Arenenberg.jpg
